references.text: Isaiah prophesied about the Messiah as the suffering servant: 'He was despised and forsaken by men' ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]). Herod's contempt and mockery of Jesus fulfill this prophecy about the Messiah being held in low esteem.
The soldiers at the cross also mocked Jesus and offered him sour wine ([ref:Luk 23:36-37|Luke 23:36-37]). The pattern of mockery and ridicule repeats throughout the story of his suffering.
In Mark's parallel account, the Roman soldiers dress Jesus in purple and mock him as king ([ref:Mark 15:17-20|Mark 15:17-20]). Herod's dressing him in a splendid robe serves the same mocking purpose.

Matthew describes the soldiers' mockery when they clothed Jesus in a scarlet robe and ridiculed him as the king of the Jews ([ref:Matt 27:27-31|Matthew 27:27-31]). This parallels Herod's mockery with the magnificent robe.

In the believers' prayer in Acts, it is mentioned that 'Herod and Pontius Pilate,' together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, gathered against Jesus ([ref:Apg 4:27-28|Acts 4:27-28]). This confirms the cooperation between Herod and Pilate in condemning Jesus.
Pilate refers to the fact that Herod also found no guilt in Jesus: 'He has done nothing deserving death' ([ref:Luk 23:15|Luke 23:15]). Despite the mockery, Herod sent Jesus back without a verdict.
Herod had long wanted to see Jesus and hoped to witness him perform a sign ([ref:Luk 23:8-9|Luke 23:8-9]). When Jesus did not answer him, Herod's curiosity turned into contempt and mockery.
On that very day, Herod and Pilate became friends, though they had previously been enemies ([ref:Luk 23:12|Luke 23:12]). The handling of the case concerning Jesus united them.
The psalmist prophetically describes how the righteous one is despised: 'All who see me mock me' ([ref:Sal 22:7-9|Psalms 22:7-9]). Herod's treatment of Jesus reflects this messianic psalm.
The soldiers wove a crown of thorns and placed a purple robe on Jesus, saying, 'Hail, king of the Jews!' ([ref:Joh 19:2-3|John 19:2-3]). As with Herod, Jesus was mocked with royal garments.
